messages.body_plain:
Agile,

On May 4, 2009, at 8:51 PM, Agile Aspect wrote:

> Simon Urbanek wrote:
>> AFAICT 32-bit is considered legacy and on Intel platforms
>
> Rubbish (on so many levels.)
>
> The only time you need a 64 bit OS is when you need a 64 bit
> address space.
>

Please consider reading more about the Intel architecture. Unlike  
other architectures 64-bit support on Intel is not merely an extension  
of the 32-bit address bus to 64-bit (such as e.g. on PowerPC which was  
designed to accommodate 64-bit address space from the beginning), but  
instead it features a new instruction set that offers performance  
gains over the old 32-bit set. Thus in general it is often beneficial  
to use 64-bit application on 64-bit-capable hardware even if you are  
not using more than 3.5GB of (virtual) memory as it has access to  
other capabilities not present in 32-bit mode. Clearly, there is still  
the trade-off of the larger pointer size, but in practice only very  
special applications get hit by that.


> I'm running both R/Eclipse/StatE on a new 32 bit Acer Aspire One
> instead of JGR because JGR is the *only* application which I run
> on it which doesn't have enough intelligence to size the display
> window to the 10 inch screen.
>

I don't quite understand what you running a legacy 32-bit PC machine  
has to do with the discussion at hand since clearly you won't benefit  
from the new instructions set (and it's not even Mac related for that  
matter).

Cheers,
Simon

messages.subject: Rserve Java Client - ints and NA
messages.subject_clean: Rserve Java Client - ints and NA
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
On R-2.9, the maximum integer is 2^31-1, the minimum integer is
-2^31+1 and -2^31 is reserved internally for NA.
Running this on the Java client(with Rserve 0.6)

r  =rc.eval("c(1,2,NA,Inf,-Inf)");
int[] dd1 = r.asIntegers();
for(int k=0;k<dd1.length;k++) System.out.print(dd1[k]+" ");

displays
1 2 0 2147483647 -2147483648

my recommendation  is that if the user requests asIntegers, NA should
be converted to  -2147483648(R's integer NA),and 2147483647 should be
converted to -2147483648 also.
that way it matches the following R code:

sapply(c(1,2,NA,Inf,-Inf),as.integer)
[1]  1  2 NA NA NA
Warning messages:
1: In lapply(X, FUN, ...) : NAs introduced by coercion
2: In lapply(X, FUN, ...) : NAs introduced by coercion


Saptarshi Guha

messages.body_plain:
On May 5, 2009, at 10:02 PM, Saptarshi Guha wrote:

> Hello,
> On R-2.9, the maximum integer is 2^31-1, the minimum integer is
> -2^31+1 and -2^31 is reserved internally for NA.
> Running this on the Java client(with Rserve 0.6)
>
> r  =rc.eval("c(1,2,NA,Inf,-Inf)");


^-- note that you are creating doubles, not integers

> int[] dd1 = r.asIntegers();
> for(int k=0;k<dd1.length;k++) System.out.print(dd1[k]+" ");
>
> displays
> 1 2 0 2147483647 -2147483648
>
> my recommendation  is that if the user requests asIntegers, NA should
> be converted to  -2147483648(R's integer NA),and 2147483647 should be
> converted to -2147483648 also.
> that way it matches the following R code:
>
> sapply(c(1,2,NA,Inf,-Inf),as.integer)
> [1]  1  2 NA NA NA
> Warning messages:
> 1: In lapply(X, FUN, ...) : NAs introduced by coercion
> 2: In lapply(X, FUN, ...) : NAs introduced by coercion
>

If that's what you want, you should use instead:
REXP r = rc.eval("as.integer(c(1,2,NA,Inf,-Inf))");

and you'll get:
1 2 -2147483648 -2147483648 -2147483648

and the last three are REXPInteger.NA values.

Converting types in Java will inherently cause problems with NAs since  
Java has no native support for NAs and dealing with them in doubles is  
messy (you have to compare binary representations). See  
REXPDouble.isNA() and REXPDouble.NA.
Having said that, I could add the check to the asInteger() conversion,  
but it will cause performance degradation, because each number will  
have to be converted to its bitwise representation to check for NAs  
which I'd rather avoid.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.subject: Re: problem with printing a question on R console afterplotting with JGR
messages.subject_clean: problem with printing a question on R console afterplotting with JGR
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The problem has to do with the console output text buffer. If the display
text is too short it gets stuck in the buffer. I'm not sure what the most
appropriate solution is, though as a dirty work around you can pad your
output.

On my machine the following works:

useless2 <- function() {
   plot(pressure)
   cat(format(" do you see the plot?\n",width=120))
   answer <- readLines(n = 1)
}
useless2()




Ian

p.s. I've cc'ed a relevant list

Sent: Tuesday, May 05, 2009 5:47 PM
To: r-sig-gui at stat.math.ethz.ch
Subject: [R-gui] problem with printing a question on R console afterplotting
with JGR

I'm using the JGR GUI on Ubuntu 9.04. The problem I'm running into is
best illustrated by the following two functions, which in theory
should be equivalent:

useless1 <- function() {
   plot(pressure)
   answer <- readline("do you see the plot?\n")
}

In JGR calling useless1() plots a graph, and at the same time a
question in the R console appears (hence I know what to answer).
However, with the following function:

useless2 <- function() {
   plot(pressure)
   cat("do you see the plot?\n")
   answer <- readLines(n = 1)
}


In JGR the plot appears but I don't see the question on the R console.
Only when I answer (without actually knowing what the question was!)
then the question appears.

This seems to be a problem with the JGR GUI, because I've never had
this problems with the Windows GUI or when running R directly from the
terminal. The problem is that some functions that I use frequently use
a similar approach than useless2() to ask interactive questions after
plotting.

Does anyone have an idea how to solve this problem (besides suggesting
another GUI)?

Many thanks,


--

messages.subject: Re: R java Graphics
messages.body_plain:
On May 19, 2009, at 12:50 PM, Bilel MASMOUDI wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I don't undertand what are event loop and how may I use them
>

REPL (read-eval-print-loop) is the way console applications usually  
work. They read (wait for input line from the user), evaluate that  
input (as expression), print the result (on the console) and loop over  
again. In order to support interactivity the loop also checks for  
events from the user interface and acts upon them. If you are using  
JRI you can use R simply by evaluating expressions in R in which case  
you are not using the R event loop so R cannot act upon them (e.g.  
when you create or resize a graphics window). You can also use JRI in  
REPL mode (by passing runMainLoop=true and corresponding  
RMainLoopCallbacks) - this is for example what JGR does.

In general it is not a good idea to use the default interactive R  
graphics devices in JRI, because they use native code that is system- 
dependent and may clash with Java's window management. That's why I'd  
strongly suggest you use JavaGD if you want to use JRI with R graphics.

Cheers,
Simon
